strengths: Timely and potentially useful problem framing: evaluating SWE agents as computer-use agents inside a real IDE is an important direction, and the paper clearly motivates why fixed tool APIs can limit generality.

PwP appears to be a practical environment design built around VSCode, Docker isolation, checkpointing, screen observations, and xdotool-style actions. This could be valuable infrastructure if released and maintained.

PwP-Bench is broad, covering 15 tasks across code editing, multimodal code generation, domain-specific programming, and non-code IDE/SWE workflows. The inclusion of IDE configuration and general SWE tasks is a nice addition beyond standard code-generation benchmarks.

The empirical analysis is informative in showing that current VLM/computer-use agents struggle badly with visual grounding, file editing, UI state tracking, and recovery from failed actions in dense IDE interfaces.
The paper usefully distinguishes primitive screenshot-based agents from agents augmented with file/bash operations and assisted high-level IDE tools, exposing where current systems gain performance.
weaknesses: The main claims are substantially overstated. The abstract and conclusion suggest computer-use agents can approach or surpass specialized tool-based agents, but the pure screenshot/mouse/keyboard setting performs very poorly overall, and the competitive numbers mostly come from adding file/bash APIs or assisted task-specific tools, which weakens the central “pixels rather than tools” thesis.

The comparison to prior state of the art is not sufficiently controlled. The paper compares against reported results from different model versions, inference budgets, prompts, pipelines, and task-specific settings, and acknowledges this issue but still uses the comparison to support strong claims.

The benchmark aggregation is questionable: macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics across very different datasets obscures task difficulty and practical significance. Some component metrics are themselves averages of multiple metrics, so the overall number is hard to interpret.

The evaluation uses PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 instances per task, which is likely too small for robust conclusions across 15 diverse benchmarks. There is little statistical analysis beyond one reported McNemar test for Intercode.

The definition of “computer-use” is blurred. Set-of-Marks annotations, DOM-derived element information, file/bash APIs, and manually engineered high-level assisted tools are all used in different settings, but the paper’s narrative sometimes treats them as evidence for one unified paradigm.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript. The code/data release line appears blank, and many important details are missing: exact prompts, action syntax constraints, SoM construction, task sampling procedure, environment images/extensions, evaluation scripts, and costs.

The new datasets, especially General-SWE and VSCode/IDE configuration tasks, are underdescribed. It is unclear how many instances they contain, how they were authored, how representative they are, and whether evaluation is robust.

Some environment claims are too broad, e.g. “all IDE tools,” full multimodal support including video/audio, and easy incorporation of future tools. The experiments mostly exercise screenshots, text, files, bash, previews, and a few IDE functions, not the full claimed space.

The assisted-tool experiment partly undermines the critique of hand-engineered APIs: performance improves substantially when task-specific APIs are manually added, but the paper frames this as evidence that agents could learn IDE tools rather than directly demonstrating such learning.

Presentation has several rough edges, including typos, table formatting issues, missing/ambiguous citations or release URL, and occasionally imprecise terminology. These do not sink the work alone, but they add to reproducibility and clarity concerns.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating software-engineering agents through realistic IDE interaction rather than only through narrow text/tool APIs.
A VSCode-based sandbox with screenshot observations, keyboard/mouse actions, checkpointing, and execution-based rewards could be a useful infrastructure contribution if released and documented well.

PwP-Bench attempts to unify a broad set of SWE-related tasks across code editing, multimodal code generation, domain-specific programming, and IDE/general SWE tasks, which is a sensible direction for stress-testing generalist agents.

The qualitative analysis of current computer-use agents is useful: the paper identifies concrete failure modes in visual grounding, file editing, IDE state understanding, tool use, and error recovery.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overstated. The paper says computer-use agents can approach or surpass specialized tool-based agents, but the pure pixel/keyboard/mouse setting performs very poorly, with the best overall average only 10.2%. The stronger 46.8% result uses file and bash APIs, which undercuts the premise of replacing hand-engineered tool interfaces with primitive IDE interaction.

The comparison to prior state of the art is not convincing. The paper aggregates heterogeneous metrics across 15 datasets, compares against individually reported SOTA numbers with different model versions, budgets, prompts, and tools, and even notes that some SOTA values are estimated. This makes the headline parity/surpass claim unreliable.

The evaluation is thin relative to the scope of the claims. Experiments are run only on PwP-Bench-Lite with 300 instances, apparently 20 per task, which is small for drawing conclusions across 15 diverse benchmarks. There is little statistical treatment beyond one isolated McNemar test.

The benchmark construction is not sufficiently specified. The paper does not clearly document sampling, task normalization, setup scripts, leakage/contamination controls, evaluator reliability, or whether the 20-sample lite subset preserves difficulty. Averaging incompatible metrics into a macro average is especially questionable.

Novelty is limited. Much of the environment appears to be a VSCode/Docker/xdotool wrapper with screenshot and SoM observations, while the benchmark largely repackages existing datasets. The paper does not clearly separate what is technically new from engineering integration.

The assisted-tool experiments muddy the contribution. Manually engineered task-specific API calls are introduced to show potential IDE-tool benefits, but this is very close to the tool-based paradigm the paper criticizes. The paper does not provide a convincing path from these oracle-like APIs to learned visual IDE tool use.

Reproducibility is weak in the manuscript. The abstract/introduction contains an apparent blank code/data release line, and many implementation details needed to reproduce the environment, prompts, SoM generation, task setup, and evaluation are missing or deferred vaguely.

The paper's positioning is too one-sided. It frames tool-based agents as fundamentally non-general, but modern systems often combine general shell/file/browser access with extensible tools. The discussion does not fairly analyze the tradeoff between low-level UI control and reliable textual APIs.

Several results actually argue against the paper's thesis: agents fail at basic file editing, cannot use many IDE features, fail to recover from errors, and perform poorly on simple General-SWE/IDE tasks. These are valuable findings, but they do not support the stronger acceptance-level claim that PwP currently demonstrates a scalable replacement paradigm.

Presentation quality has issues, including typos, formatting artifacts, unclear legends, and imprecise claims such as support for video/audio despite not evaluating those modalities. These issues reduce confidence in the care of the benchmark and experimental protocol.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and timely gap: SWE agents are usually evaluated through task-specific tool APIs, while real developers operate in rich IDE environments. A VSCode-based computer-use environment is a meaningful contribution for studying general-purpose coding agents.

PwP-Bench is broad in scope, combining 15 tasks across code editing, multimodal code generation, domain-specific programming, and non-code IDE workflows. This breadth is valuable and goes beyond the usual pull-request or code-generation-only evaluations.

The experimental results are informative even when performance is low. The contrast between primitive UI agents, file/bash-assisted agents, and domain-tool-assisted agents highlights concrete bottlenecks in current VLM agents: visual grounding, file editing, recovery from mistakes, and underuse of IDE functionality.

The qualitative failure analysis is a strong part of the paper. The examples of hallucinated UI state, wrong clicks, active-panel confusion, and poor debugger/tool use make the benchmark’s difficulty and research value convincing.

The environment design appears practically useful: sandboxed containers, VSCode integration, screenshots/video, xdotool actions, checkpointing, and execution-based evaluation make it a plausible platform for future SWE-agent research.
weaknesses: The main empirical claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. The paper says computer-use agents can approach or outperform prior state of the art, but the headline 46.8% result relies on file/bash API access, not purely pixel-based IDE interaction, and comparisons to prior SOTA mix different budgets, model versions, tools, and metrics.

Evaluation is limited to PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 examples per task. This is understandable for cost reasons, but it creates high variance and weakens claims about broad benchmark performance, especially when per-task success rates are often near zero or based on small counts.

The aggregation methodology is underjustified. Averaging heterogeneous metrics across HumanEval, SWE-Bench, ChartMimic, DSBench, BIRD, theorem proving, and IDE tasks can obscure what the overall score means; some metrics are themselves averages of submetrics, making the macro-average hard to interpret.

The benchmark contribution is partly a unification of existing datasets, but the paper does not provide enough detail about task adaptation, sampling, potential contamination, evaluation scripts, or how faithfully original benchmark conditions are preserved. The two new task sets also need more specification and validation.

The comparison between tool-based and computer-use paradigms is not fully clean. PwP itself exposes DOM state, VSCode extension APIs, file/bash operations, and manually engineered assisted APIs in some settings, so the boundary between environment affordances and hand-engineered agent tools needs sharper treatment.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as written: the abstract says code and data are released, but the release location appears blank. More details on prompts, SoM generation, action syntax, model versions, costs, random seeds, failed executions, and per-task confidence intervals would be needed.

Some novelty claims are overstated. General GUI/OS agent environments already exist, and the core novelty is specifically SWE-focused IDE packaging plus benchmark adaptation rather than a fundamentally new agent method. The paper would be stronger with a more modest positioning.

The primitive pixel-only results are very low, which supports the benchmark’s difficulty but also undercuts the strongest thesis that computer-use agents are currently competitive without hand-engineered tools. The most successful setting still depends heavily on non-visual file and shell access.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely question: whether general computer-use agents can perform realistic software engineering through an IDE, rather than through bespoke coding-agent APIs.

The proposed PwP environment is a meaningful contribution: a VSCode-based, visually controlled, sandboxed, execution-evaluated setup with support for screenshots, DOM/state access, file system verification, checkpointing, and a gym-like API.

PwP-Bench is broad and ambitious, combining 15 task sources across code generation, pull-request repair, multimodal code synthesis, data science, SQL, theorem proving, CTF-style tasks, IDE configuration, and general SWE tasks.

The empirical study covers a useful range of closed and open models, pure visual CUAs, CUAs augmented with file/bash APIs, and a specialized SWE-agent baseline, yielding several informative findings about visual grounding, file editing, IDE tool use, and the gap between visual and text/API-based interaction.

The qualitative failure analysis is useful and actionable: the paper identifies concrete failure modes such as wrong UI element selection, hallucinated screen state, poor recovery from failed actions, and inability to exploit IDE refactoring/debugging/profiling tools.
The work is likely to be useful as an evaluation platform for future CUA and SWE-agent research, especially if the claimed code/data release is complete and maintained.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is on PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 instances per task, despite the full benchmark containing 5400 instances. This makes several per-dataset numbers noisy, especially for difficult tasks with many 0%, 5%, or 10% entries, and the paper provides almost no confidence intervals or significance analysis.

The comparison to specialized SWE agents is not fully satisfying. The only systematically evaluated specialized baseline is MiniSweAgent, while the paper also discusses best-reported results gathered from citations, leaderboards, and even a web-search agent. These comparisons are acknowledged as imperfect but still used to motivate claims, and they are not controlled for sample selection, model version, inference budget, or evaluation split.

The 20-step cap in the main experiments is a substantial confound for SWE tasks, especially SWE-Bench-like tasks. Although an appendix reports 250-step results for three datasets, the main benchmark conclusions still rely heavily on a horizon that may systematically disadvantage visual agents and long-horizon coding agents in different ways.

The macro-average over very heterogeneous tasks and metrics is hard to interpret. Some tasks use accuracy, others average multiple visual/layout metrics, and DSBench uses normalized competition scores. Equal weighting across datasets and metrics may not reflect task difficulty, importance, or statistical reliability.

The distinction between a computer-use agent with file/bash APIs and a specialized coding agent becomes blurry. The large performance jump from adding file editing and bash APIs is interesting, but it partly weakens the central framing around visual IDE use, since some strong results come from bypassing the visual interface rather than using it.

Several central claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, claims about approaching specialist-level performance, rapid progress over time, and latent IDE-tool abilities are based on limited samples, selected model families, or assisted/tool-guided experiments rather than a comprehensive causal analysis.

The paper has clarity and polish issues that undermine confidence: repeated typos, inconsistent terminology, crowded tables, and at least one apparent inconsistency in the reported visual-grounding error rates between the main text and appendix.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript. The paper claims code and data release, but the visible release URL/location is not clear in the extracted text, and important details about prompts, task sampling, exact verifiers, environment images, and cost/inference budgets would need to be fully available for the benchmark to be trustworthy.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely question: whether general computer-use agents can perform realistic software engineering through an IDE rather than through specialized tool APIs.

A VSCode-based environment with visual interaction, DOM/Set-of-Marks support, sandboxing, checkpointing, and programmatic verification could be a useful infrastructure contribution if released and maintained well.

The benchmark attempts broad coverage across code editing, multimodal code generation, data science, CTF, theorem proving, SQL, IDE configuration, and general SWE tasks, which is more diverse than many narrow code benchmarks.

The empirical result that pure visual interaction performs much worse than file/bash API access is plausible and relevant, and the paper includes useful qualitative failure modes around visual grounding, UI state hallucination, and poor recovery.
The evaluation includes a reasonably wide set of frontier and open-weight multimodal/computer-use models, which gives a useful snapshot of current capabilities.
weaknesses: The core empirical evidence is much weaker than the paper's claims. Although PwP-Bench has 5400 instances, the main evaluation uses only PwP-Bench-Lite with 300 instances, apparently 20 random examples per task, with no confidence intervals, variance estimates, sensitivity to sampling, or evidence that the subset preserves difficulty beyond assertion.

The benchmark contribution is overstated. Most tasks are ports or aggregations of existing datasets, while the genuinely new IDE/general-SWE components appear tiny in the full benchmark (20 VSCode and 20 General SWE instances). Claiming a comprehensive benchmark for broad SWE skills is hard to justify from so few new non-code/IDE-specific tasks.

The overall metric is poorly justified. The paper macro-averages heterogeneous metrics across tasks, including accuracy, CLIP/design metrics, chart metrics, normalized Kaggle scores, and averages of SWT-Bench submetrics. This creates an aggregate score whose interpretation is unclear and can obscure large differences in task validity, scale, and difficulty.

Comparisons to specialized SWE agents are inadequate. The main table includes only MiniSweAgent with Claude-4.0 as the specialized baseline, while stronger specialized systems are discussed only through non-comparable reported numbers from different subsets, prompts, models, pipelines, and dates. This does not support strong claims about approaching or matching specialist-level performance.

The 20-step cap is a major confound for SWE tasks such as SWE-Bench. The appendix's 250-step experiment is limited to only three datasets and a few agents, and it actually changes some conclusions substantially. The main evaluation therefore mixes short-horizon UI tasks with long-horizon SWE tasks under an artificial budget that may not reflect realistic agent performance.

The paper contains internal inconsistencies and presentation errors that undermine confidence. For example, the visual grounding error rates are reversed between the main text and appendix, Table 8 is referenced for different experiments, and there are numerous typos and formatting issues. These are not merely cosmetic when they affect reported analysis.

The assisted-tool experiment is under-specified and risks circularity: the authors manually engineer IDE-based tool calls, then argue that agents could in principle learn these through UI actions. This does not cleanly measure current CUA ability, nor does it establish that the visual environment alone is an effective interface.

Several claims are unsupported or exaggerated, including that PwP gives agents access to the full spectrum of developer tools in a fair way, that PwP-Bench-Lite preserves the full benchmark distribution and difficulty, and that the environment enables direct comparison between CUAs and specialized agents. In practice, different agents receive different observations, APIs, prompts, and modalities.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a benchmark/environment paper. The paper says code and data are released, but the manuscript does not provide enough detail about task conversion, exact prompts, verifier reliability, environment images, seeds, sampling procedure, cost, failure handling, and whether all third-party datasets can be redistributed.

Ethical and safety considerations are largely absent despite including CTF/ethical hacking tasks, code execution in sandboxes, and automated software modification. The sandbox is mentioned technically, but misuse and benchmark leakage/contamination risks are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: evaluating whether general computer-use agents can do realistic software engineering through an IDE is an important question with clear implications for both GUI agents and SWE agents.

The proposed PwP environment is well motivated: a VSCode-based, Dockerized, gym-style interface with screenshot/DOM/action channels, checkpointing, execution-based verification, and support for IDE tools provides a useful platform for future research.

PwP-Bench is broad, covering 15 tasks, multiple languages, multimodal inputs, code generation/editing, domain-specific programming, IDE configuration, and general SWE activities. This breadth is a real contribution compared with narrower SWE or OS benchmarks.

The empirical results are informative and actionable: pure visual CUAs perform poorly, file/bash APIs close much of the gap, and assisted IDE-tool APIs suggest that better tool use and visual grounding are key bottlenecks.

The paper evaluates a strong set of current models, including closed and open vision-language/UI agents, and includes task-wise results, qualitative failure analysis, and a longer-horizon check on SWE-Bench-like tasks.
weaknesses: The benchmark contribution is partly an aggregation/porting of existing datasets, with only two newly created task sets. The novelty is therefore strongest as an environment/unification effort rather than as a fundamentally new evaluation methodology.

The main evaluation uses PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 examples per task. This is understandable for cost, but it weakens claims about overall benchmark performance and makes several task-level comparisons statistically fragile.

The overall macro-average combines heterogeneous metrics across tasks, including accuracy, CLIP-like visual metrics, averages of multiple dataset-specific metrics, and normalized competition scores. This makes the single overall score hard to interpret.

The specialized-agent comparison is limited. MiniSweAgent is the only directly evaluated SWE baseline, while comparisons to best reported specialized systems are not on the same subset and are explicitly not directly comparable. This limits the strength of claims about approaching or matching specialist agents.

The 20-step cap may disproportionately penalize pure computer-use agents on long-horizon SWE tasks. The 250-step appendix helps, but only covers three SWE-Bench-related datasets and one main model family.
Some new task categories, especially General-SWE and VSCode tasks, are small and not specified in enough detail to fully assess difficulty, diversity, and reproducibility from the manuscript alone.

There are presentation and consistency issues, including a missing code/data URL in the footnote and an apparent contradiction in reported visual-grounding error rates between the main text and appendix.

The paper would be stronger with more rigorous uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests across the 20-instance-per-task evaluations, especially given the many near comparisons between agents.
